_note: Example output produced by IncidentIQ from the input files in this same folder (examples/course-registration). Model output is not deterministic; a fresh run may differ in wording and confidence values.

summary.summary: At 20:00 the course-registration window opened and request volume rose from roughly 180 to 2400 requests per second. Within 30 seconds average latency climbed from about 210ms to over 8 seconds. The registration API reported a 96% cache miss rate on course-capacity keys, forcing each request to recompute seat availability from the database, where a seats_remaining query performing a full table scan on enrollments took over 6 seconds. Database CPU reached 97% with more than 400 slow-query entries. No deployment occurred today.

facts.statement: Request volume increased from 180/s before the window to 2400/s at 20:00:04.
Average latency rose to 8200ms by 20:00:22 and 9100ms by 20:03.
Cache miss rate on course:capacity:* keys reached 96%.
facts.evidence: 20:00:30 WARN reg-api cache MISS rate 96% on key course:capacity:*

facts.statement: A seats_remaining query took 6100ms and performed a full table scan on enrollments.
facts.evidence: 20:00:45 ERROR reg-api db query seats_remaining took 6100ms (full table scan on enrollments)

facts.statement: reg-db CPU reached 97% with over 400 slow-query log entries.
facts.evidence: 20:01:10 WARN reg-db CPU 97%, slow query log 400+ entries

facts.statement: No deployment occurred in the last five days; course capacity is cached in Redis with a 30-second TTL.
facts.evidence: Deployment notes: No deploy in the last 5 days; capacity cached in Redis with 30s TTL, cache is cold at window open.

assumptions.statement: The enrollments table lacks an index supporting the seats_remaining query.
assumptions.why: The log reports a full table scan, which strongly implies a missing index, but no schema information appears in the input.

assumptions.statement: The index-less admin query added six days ago is related to the current slow query.
assumptions.why: The deployment note mentions an index-less query on enrollments, but does not confirm it is the same query path used by seats_remaining.

assumptions.statement: Redis itself was healthy and the misses were genuine cold-cache misses.
assumptions.why: A 96% miss rate is consistent with a cold cache, but a Redis outage or eviction would look similar and no Redis health data is provided.

assumptions.statement: This degradation is specific to peak load rather than a permanent regression.
assumptions.why: Latency was normal at 19:58, but the input covers only a few minutes of history.

timeline.event: Normal operation: 180 requests/s at 210ms average latency.
Registration window opens; traffic jumps to 2400 requests/s.
Redis capacity cache is cold, since entries expire on a 30s TTL and no traffic pre-warmed them.
timeline.source: inferred from deployment note on TTL and cold cache

timeline.event: Cache miss rate on capacity keys measured at 96%.
Capacity lookup for CS101 misses and falls back to recomputing from the database.
seats_remaining query takes 6100ms via a full table scan on enrollments.
reg-db CPU at 97% with 400+ slow queries logged.
Traffic still at 2100/s with latency at 9100ms; no recovery.

hypotheses.title: Cold cache at window open converted every request into an expensive unindexed database query
supporting: 96% cache miss rate measured immediately after the window opened
Capacity cache uses a 30s TTL and was cold at open, per the deployment notes
Each miss recomputes seats_remaining, which is logged at 6100ms with a full table scan
Database CPU reached 97% with 400+ slow queries, consistent with mass fallback to the database
contradicting: No Redis health metrics are provided, so the misses could have another cause
The input does not confirm the miss rate stayed high after the first seconds
hypotheses.test: Pre-warm the capacity cache before the next window and compare miss rate, latency, and database CPU.

hypotheses.title: A missing index on enrollments makes the seats_remaining query unable to survive peak load
supporting: The query is explicitly logged as a full table scan taking 6100ms
An index-less query on enrollments was added six days ago per the deployment notes
Database CPU saturates rather than the application tier
contradicting: The system ran normally at 180 requests/s with the same schema, so the index alone does not explain the failure
No schema or EXPLAIN output is present in the input to confirm which index is missing
hypotheses.test: Run EXPLAIN on the seats_remaining query, add the appropriate index in staging, and re-run a load test at 2400 requests/s.

hypotheses.title: Raw traffic volume exceeds provisioned capacity regardless of caching
supporting: Traffic rose more than thirteenfold, from 180/s to 2400/s
Latency remained above 9 seconds at 20:03 with traffic still at 2100/s
contradicting: The specific bottleneck logged is a slow database query, not saturated application instances or a connection limit
A working cache would absorb most of this traffic without reaching the database at all
hypotheses.test: Replay the same traffic volume with a warm cache and an indexed query; if latency stays high, capacity is the real constraint.

hypotheses.title: Redis outage or eviction rather than a genuinely cold cache
supporting: A 96% miss rate is extreme even for a cold cache
contradicting: A 30s TTL with no pre-window traffic fully explains a cold cache without any failure
No Redis errors, connection failures, or memory warnings appear anywhere in the input
hypotheses.test: Check Redis memory usage, eviction counters, and error logs for the 19:55-20:05 window.

risks.where: With no deploy today, the investigation may default to 'it is just load' because traffic spikes are the familiar explanation for slowness at peak.
risks.mitigation: Follow the specific bottleneck named in the logs — a 6-second unindexed query — rather than the most familiar story.

risks.where: The index-less query added six days ago is tempting to name as the cause simply because it came before, even though the system ran normally for six days.
risks.mitigation: Explain why the change was harmless for six days; a latent factor exposed by load is not the same as a trigger.

risks.where: The cold-cache story is elegant, so the equally plausible possibility of a Redis eviction or outage may never be checked.
risks.mitigation: Pull Redis health metrics explicitly, even though the cold-cache explanation already fits.

risks.where: Cold cache, missing index, and peak traffic are each insufficient alone; the incident requires all three together.
risks.mitigation: State the causal chain as a conjunction and test each link separately rather than searching for one root cause.

risks.where: This analysis reads confidently, yet key elements such as the missing index are inferred from a single log phrase.
risks.mitigation: Confirm the schema with EXPLAIN before treating the missing index as established fact.

actions.action: Run EXPLAIN on the seats_remaining query and confirm which index is missing on enrollments.
actions.link: Tests H2; converts the central assumption into a measured fact

actions.action: Pre-warm the course-capacity cache a few minutes before the next registration window.
actions.link: Directly tests H1 and is the cheapest immediate mitigation

actions.action: Raise the capacity cache TTL well above 30 seconds, or refresh it in the background rather than on demand.
actions.link: Removes the repeated cold-start behaviour identified in H1

actions.action: Pull Redis memory, eviction, and error metrics for 19:55-20:05.
actions.link: Rules H4 in or out; currently unchecked

actions.action: Load-test at 2400 requests/s in staging with a warm cache and the new index before the next window.
actions.link: Distinguishes H1 and H2 from the pure-capacity explanation in H3

questions: Which index is actually missing, and is the admin query from six days ago on the same code path as seats_remaining?
Was Redis healthy throughout, or were keys being evicted under memory pressure?
What did the previous registration window look like — is this a regression or a recurring pattern?
How long did the degradation last, and did the system recover on its own once the cache warmed?
Were any registrations lost or duplicated while the system was timing out?

devil.counter: The cold-cache explanation is assumed rather than measured, and a Redis failure would produce identical symptoms with a completely different fix.
points: A 96% miss rate is higher than a cold cache alone would typically produce once the first few requests populate entries — after 30 seconds of 2400 requests/s, hit rates should have recovered, yet latency was still climbing at 20:03.
There is no Redis health data whatsoever in the evidence. Memory pressure and key eviction under load would look exactly like a cold cache from the application side.
The full table scan is reported in a single log line. Nobody has run EXPLAIN, and the connection to the admin query added six days ago is an association, not a demonstrated code path.
If load alone were sufficient to saturate the database, pre-warming the cache would help far less than the leading hypothesis predicts — and that outcome would not be visible until the next window.
devil.blindspot: Committing to cold cache plus missing index means never pulling Redis metrics. If keys were being evicted under memory pressure, adding an index and pre-warming would reduce the symptom while leaving the real fault in place until the next peak.
